facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
The applicant joined the demonstration of 19 July 1989 as a reporter for the newspaper Exormisis.
While the applicant was trying to help some of the women demonstrators, he was grabbed and beaten by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was taken at gunpoint together with others who had also been arrested during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
At around 2.30 a.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant and some other men were ordered onto a police bus.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days following the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
On 22 July 1989, the applicant was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (CYP) – approximately 85 euros (EUR).

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the "TRNC".

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, Turkish forces started to beat some women demonstrators with batons, to kick them and drag them by the arms, legs and hair.
While the applicant was trying to help some of the women demonstrators, he was grabbed and beaten by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was hit in the face and other parts of the body by Turkish policemen during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant's photographic equipment was seized despite him showing his press card during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was led to a bus through an angry crowd of 200-300 civilians who shouted abuse and threats at him.
As the applicant was walking without police protection, the crowd had an opportunity to rush at him, and he was dragged and beaten until two policemen came and accompanied him onto the bus.
While at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", the applicant saw a policeman in civilian clothes who told him "Turkey will kill you".
The applicant was taken to the Seray Police Station, where, after a body search, he was held in a cell that was filthy, dirty and dark.
On 26 July 1989, the applicant was locked in an isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison as punishment for refusing food.
The isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison in which the applicant was placed on 26 July 1989 was extremely small and unbearably hot (40-60°C).
In support of his claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced five medical certificates.

The applicant alleged that his health problems (osteoarthritis of the cervical cord, cervical disc disease, and related conditions) were the result of the savage blows he had received from Turkish policemen, soldiers and civilians in July 1989.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.
The applicant produced 21 photographs taken at different times during the demonstration on 19 July 1989.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.

Before the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court passed sentence, the Bishop of Kitium, speaking on behalf of all the accused, made a statement saying that their struggle was peaceful, that their aim was to encourage Greek and Turkish-Cypriots to live together in peace, that they carried no weapons and that they had asked for UN protection.
